question: An FD offers 7.2% per annum compounded quarterly. What is the Effective Annual Rate (EAR)?
before: EAR = (1 + 0.072/4)^4 - 1 = (1.018)^4 - 1 = 7.396% ≈ 7.40%. A is the nominal rate. C rounds incorrectly. D overestimates the compounding benefit.
after:
Formula: EAR = (1 + r/m)^m − 1, where r = nominal annual rate, m = compounding frequency per year.

Step-by-step: The nominal rate is 7.2% per annum compounded quarterly, so r = 0.072 and m = 4.

Substitute into the formula: EAR = (1 + 0.072/4)^4 − 1 = (1 + 0.018)^4 − 1 = (1.018)^4 − 1.

Calculate (1.018)^4 = 1.073964 (approximately), then subtract 1 to get 0.073964.

Result: 0.073964 or 7.3964%, which rounds to 7.40%.

Why this is correct: The effective annual rate accounts for the benefit of quarterly compounding. Each quarter, interest is calculated and reinvested, generating interest-on-interest. The formula (1 + r/m)^m correctly compounds the nominal rate m times across the year and reveals the true annual return.

Why the others are wrong:

A (7.20%): This is simply the nominal (stated) annual rate. It ignores the effect of quarterly compounding and does not capture the additional return generated by reinvesting interest within the year.

C (7.39%): This appears to round 7.3964% down rather than to the nearest hundredth. Standard rounding of 7.3964% is 7.40%, not 7.39%.

D (7.50%): This significantly overestimates the compounding benefit. It suggests a higher frequency or a higher nominal rate than actually exists and misapplies the compounding formula.

Intuition: In equity and fixed-income analysis, nominal rates advertised by banks or issuers can be misleading. The EAR is the true cost of capital or return on investment because it reflects what you actually earn when interest compounds during the year. An analyst must always convert to EAR to make fair comparisons across instruments with different compounding frequencies.
